messages.subject: Re: plot size not "maintained" by grid.arrange
messages.body_plain:
Ellen,

Your plots are calling for variables that do not exist in your provided datasets. They look almost like you want the residuals from a lm() between two variables, but your dataset only has the two variables so I cannot reproduce. I edited your script and put it into the attached. theme_ellen() seemed appropriate given that you were repeating the same changes to the grid lines in every plot. Also, it got rid of those annoying warnings.

Can you supply values or supply the code that you use to compute your residuals?

Brandon

messages.subject: Re: plot size not "maintained" by grid.arrange
messages.body_plain:
What version of ggplot2 are you running? I have no issues with %replace%.
sessionInfo()
Mine is below.

The reason why you're plot is compressed is because it is cramming the plot and the legend into the area you supplied via gridExtra. The best thing to do is to get rid of the legend and your plot will then take up the space. Thanks to Baptiste's good documentation and examples I found this:

https://code.google.com/p/gridextra/wiki/arrangeGrob

Which allowed me to edit the script. Should work and look snazzy now!

B

messages.subject: Upcoming R training: SF Dec 3-4, DC Dec 10-11
messages.subject_clean: Upcoming R training: SF Dec 3-4, DC Dec 10-11
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'd like to let you know about four R training courses that RStudio
will be offering in December:

* Effective data visualization (http://bit.ly/TY2ONI)
  Dec 3. San Francisco, CA

* Reports and reproducible research (http://bit.ly/RsZmYr)
  Dec 4. San Francisco, CA

* Advanced R programming (http://bit.ly/RvZDsd)
  Dec 10. Washington, DC

* Package development (http://bit.ly/UhTIWz)
  Dec 11. Washington, DC

In EFFECTIVE DATA VISUALISATION (http://bit.ly/TY2ONI), you'll learn
how to make beautiful, effective graphs using ggplot2 and the grammar
of graphics. You'll learn not only technical R skills, but also how
the human perceptual system works. REPORTS AND REPRODUCIBLE RESEARCH
(http://bit.ly/RsZmYr) will jump start your workflow for generating
polished and reproducible publications and presentations from R
research. You'll learn how to use knitr to make scriptable pdf
reports, html pages and slideshows, and general tips for making code
that others can use and learn from.

ADVANCED R PROGRAMMING (http://bit.ly/RvZDsd) will help you write
better code, by focussing on the mantra of "do not repeat yourself".
You will learn powerful new tools of abstraction, allowing you to
solve a wider range of problems with fewer lines of code. PACKAGE

Hello,

I have a question concerning geom_rect (that works not how I expect) and geom_segment (that works but I dont want it because ... it is geom_segment - I dont want diagonal lines. I want "rectangles").

segment-syntax:
> ggplot (df) + facet_grid (type~., scales="free_y")+ geom_point(aes(x=start.ens, y=fc.trans)) + geom_segment(aes (x=start.ens, xend=end.ens, y=0, yend=peak))+ geom_segment(aes (x=start.ens, xend=end.grcm38, y=0, yend=dpeak))

It is the same for a less complex syntax without facet_grid etc.:
> ggplot (df) + geom_segment(aes (x=start.ens, xend=end.grcm38, y=0, yend=dpeak))

rect-syntax:
ggplot (df) + facet_grid (type~., scales="free_y")+ geom_point(aes(x=start.ens, y=fc.trans)) + geom_rect(aes (xmin=start.ens, xmax=end.ens, ymin=0, ymax=peak))+ geom_rect(aes (xmin=start.ens, xmax=end.grcm38, ymin=0, ymax=dpeak))

Hm, maybe it's because I'm using the latest development version of ggplot2, but mine doesn't have the hole in the middle when I use width=1.

Now that I think of it, with ggplot2 0.9.2.1, you might be able to make it work by using scale_x_discrete(expand=c(0, 0)):

library(ggplot2)
dat <- data.frame(y = c(0.08, 0.92), g = c("A", "B"))

ggplot(dat, aes(x = factor(1), y = y, fill = g)) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity", width=1) +

  scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y")

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Re-ordering by multi-dimensional data for ggplot2 plotting
messages.subject_clean: Re-ordering by multi-dimensional data for ggplot2 plotting
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ed,

The answer you received on Stack Overflow is basically the way I would
do it. Here is my variant:

mydata$Instance <- with(mydata, {
  factor(Instance,
         levels=levels(reorder(Instance[System=="a"],
                               Value[System=="a"])))
})

qplot(data=mydata, weight=Value, Instance, fill=System, position="dodge")

This may not be the "most elegant" way, but in my experience R is
often a bit inelegant. You can always fake elegance by hiding the
complexity, e.g.

reorder2 <- function(data, x, y, sub.var, sub.value) {
  factor(data[[x]],
  levels = levels(
    reorder(
      data[data[[sub.var]] == sub.value, x],
      data[data[[sub.var]] == sub.value, y])))
}

qplot(data=mydata,
      weight=Value,
      reorder2(mydata,
               "Instance",
               "Value",
               "System",
               "a"),
      fill=System,
      position="dodge")

Best,
Ista

FYI, with R Under development (unstable) (2012-11-01 r61067), I get an error that I think is related to recent updates on S4 in R devel, e.g.

"setRefClass() and getRefClass() now return class generator functions, similar to setClass(), but still with the reference fields and methods as before (suggestion of Romain Francois)." [http://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/NEWS.R-devel.html]

I post it here, in case it's something that ggplot2 is doing incorrectly (although I don't think so).  If not, feel free to report/forward this to the R devel mailing list.

> library(ggplot2)
> example(ggplot)

ggplot+                  y = rnorm(30))

ggplot> library(plyr)
ggplot> ds <- ddply(df, .(gp), summarise, mean = mean(y), sd = sd(y))
ggplot> # Declare the data frame and common aesthetics.
ggplot> # The summary data frame ds is used to plot
ggplot> # larger red points in a second geom_point() layer.
ggplot> # If the data = argument is not specified, it uses the
ggplot> # declared data frame from ggplot(); ditto for the aesthetics.
ggplot> ggplot(df, aes(x = gp, y = y)) +

Brad Horn <bxh...@gmail.com> Nov 01 08:53AM -0700

Here is the code from the book:

(unemp <- qplot(date, unemploy, data=economics, geom="line",
xlab = "", ylab = "No. unemployed (1000s)"))

presidential <- presidential[-(1:3), ]

yrng <- range(economics$unemploy)
xrng <- range(economics$date)
unemp + geom_vline(aes(xintercept = start), data = presidential)

When I run the last line above, I do NOT get vertical lines as expected.
Instead I get the following error:

Error: Discrete value supplied to continuous scale

Why?

Brad Horn <bxh...@gmail.com> Nov 02 05:10AM -0700

A simple reply confirmed that the start data used in the intercept argument
needs to be changed from a date to a numeric object. This faithfully
reproduces the example in the book.

On Thursday, November 1, 2012 11:53:52 AM UTC-4, Brad Horn wrote:

 geo_vline: Error in example from ggplot2 book (p86) <http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/t/93545baddc4bb10f>

Brad Horn <bxh...@gmail.com> Nov 01 11:13AM -0700

The following code appears in the book (p86) and the book website to
illustrates the use of geom_vline:

unemp <- qplot(date, unemploy, data=economics, geom="line", xlab = "", ylab
= "No. unemployed (1000s)")
presidential <- presidential[-(1:3), ]
yrng <- range(economics$unemploy)
xrng <- range(economics$date)
unemp + geom_vline(aes(xintercept = start), data = presidential)

In my case, I geom_vline is generating the following error:

Error: Discrete value supplied to continuous scale

Logic says I shouldn't get this error. Any help or insight is appreciated
as I want to ensure the chart annotations are feasible.

Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> Nov 01 09:17PM -0700

Hi:

> str(presidential)
'data.frame': 7 obs. of 4 variables:
$ name : chr "Nixon" "Ford" "Carter" "Reagan" ...
$ start: Date, format: "1969-01-20" "1974-08-09" ...
$ end : Date, format: "1974-08-09" "1977-01-20" ...
$ party: chr "Republican" "Republican" "Democratic" "Republican" ...

Observe that start is a Date object - you want the numeric equivalent,
because that's what is really plotted. This works for me in version 0.9.2.1 <http://0.9.2.1>:

unemp + geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.numeric(start)), data = presidential)

Dennis

Then you can run the same plot command and it will work.

messages.subject: Release candidates for plyr 1.8 and ggplot2 0.9.3
messages.subject_clean: Release candidates for plyr 1.8 and ggplot2 0.9.3
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

(We've bcc'd everyone who's a maintainer of a package that depends, imports or suggests ggplot2 or plyr.)

We have prepared release candidates (RCs) for plyr 1.8 and ggplot2 0.9.3, which we plan to release to CRAN simultaneously. Unless there are major unexpected bugs, they will be in the RC phase for a about a month before they are sent to CRAN on December 1.

The purpose of the RC phase is to uncover unexpected bugs in ggplot2 and plyr. These releases do not include any changes that we expect to break existing code, but we hope that this period will allows to uncover any unexpected changes and remedying them before releasing to CRAN. The next version of ggplot2 (0.9.3) contains primarily bugfixes, while the next version of plyr (1.8) has a number of new features and performance enhancements. For the full list of changes, see:

  https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/master/NEWS
  https://github.com/hadley/plyr/blob/master/NEWS

It would be very helpful if you could try out the RC version and see if it breaks any of your existing code.  To try out the the new versions, run the following code:

  install.packages("devtools")
  library(devtools)
  install_github("plyr", ref = "plyr-1.8-rc")
  install_github("gtable", ref = "gtable-0.1.2-rc")
  install_github("scales", ref = "scales-0.2.3-rc")
  install_github("ggplot2", ref = "ggplot2-0.9.3-rc")

After installation has completed, you will need to restart R. Then you can test your existing code that uses plyr and ggplot2.

Installation notes:

This will install plyr from source, which requires that you have a C compiler on your system. Please see this page for information about that (it also describes installing LaTeX, but that's not necessary here):

  http://www.rstudio.com/ide/docs/packages/prerequisites

Installing with dev_mode():

Installing the RC versions of these packages is slightly different from usual. Unlike the usual method, these can NOT be installed with the dev_mode() function from devtools, which is normally used to keep development and released packages separate. This is because devtools indirectly depends on plyr and when you load devtools, it will load the version of plyr in your normal library (not your development library). Thus the new version of plyr must be installed NOT in dev_mode(). (If you really require a workaround for this, it is possible; please send an email to the manipulatr mailing list.)

If you encounter any problems with the new version, please post to either the ggplot2-dev or manipulatr mailing lists, or file an issue on Github.

Thanks!
Winston Chang
Hadley Wickham

messages.subject: Improve graphic "grooming"
messages.body_plain:
Dear plotter colleagues,

  I am really novice in ggplot2 and I'm struggling to improve a graphic. Here is the code I use to produce my plot:

p <- ggplot(a, aes(x=year, y=value, fill=as.factor(class)))
p + geom_bar(position="fill", width=0.5) +
    labs(x= 'Year', y= 'Proportion') +
    scale_colour_brewer(palette=5, name='Classes') +
    theme(legend.title=element_text(face = "italic"))

  and it yields this graphic: http://imageshack.us/content_round.php?page=done&l=img194/1445/outrb.png

  However, there are a few things that I would like to improve. For example:

messages.subject: Re: Problem using shape and fill
messages.body_plain:
On 11/5/2012 9:27 AM, Mark wrote:
> I can't find an explanation or work around for a problem I'm having
> when I use map one variable to shape and another to fill. The below
> example seems to ignore fill entirely.
>
> ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg)) +
>    geom_point(aes(shape=factor(vs), fill=factor(am)), size=4) +
>    scale_shape_discrete(solid=FALSE)
>
> This example plots correctly but the legend is incorrect
>
> ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg)) +
>    geom_point(aes(shape=factor(vs), fill=factor(am)), size=4) +
>    scale_shape_manual(values=c(21, 23))

The solid=FALSE argument to scale_shape_discrete does not do what you
think it does; it selects solid shapes (ones that have the same middle
color as they are drawn in) rather than fillable shapes (ones which can
have a different fill color than line color.

For a catalog of all the shapes and the effects of color and fill on
them, try:

DF <- data.frame(pt = 0:25, x = 1, y = 1)
ggplot(DF, aes(x=x, y=y, shape=pt)) +
   geom_point(colour="red", fill="lightblue", size=10) +
   scale_shape_identity() +
   facet_wrap(~pt) +
   theme_bw() +
   theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
         axis.title = element_blank(),
         axis.ticks = element_blank())

Requesting solid shapes (the default) gives 16, 17, 15, 3, 7, and 8.
Requesting not solid shapes gives 1, 2, 0, 3, 7, 8. Neither set includes
the fillable ones (21-25), so you have to specify them using a manual
scale as you do in your second example.

The problem with the legend in the second example is that the shape of
the points in the legend is, by default, 16. But fill does not have an
effect of shape 16, so the legend is all black circles. Shape 21 is a
better choice and that can be specified with

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg)) +
   geom_point(aes(shape=factor(vs), fill=factor(am)), size=4) +

   scale_shape_manual(values=c(21, 23)) +
   scale_fill_discrete(guide = guide_legend(override.aes = aes(shape = 21)))

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

I've been asked how to use the new version of plyr with dev_mode. It requires one extra step, and I've written it up here:

-Winston

On Mon, Nov 5, 2012 at 11:56 AM, Winston Chang <winsto...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi everyone -
>
> (We've bcc'd everyone who's a maintainer of a package that depends, imports or suggests ggplot2 or plyr.)
>
> We have prepared release candidates (RCs) for plyr 1.8 and ggplot2 0.9.3, which we plan to release to CRAN simultaneously. Unless there are major unexpected bugs, they will be in the RC phase for a about a month before they are sent to CRAN on December 1.
>
> The purpose of the RC phase is to uncover unexpected bugs in ggplot2 and plyr. These releases do not include any changes that we expect to break existing code, but we hope that this period will allows to uncover any unexpected changes and remedying them before releasing to CRAN. The next version of ggplot2 (0.9.3) contains primarily bugfixes, while the next version of plyr (1.8) has a number of new features and performance enhancements. For the full list of changes, see:
>
>   https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/master/NEWS
>   https://github.com/hadley/plyr/blob/master/NEWS
>
> It would be very helpful if you could try out the RC version and see if it breaks any of your existing code.  To try out the the new versions, run the following code:
>
>   install.packages("devtools")
>   library(devtools)
>   install_github("plyr", ref = "plyr-1.8-rc")
>   install_github("gtable", ref = "gtable-0.1.2-rc")
>   install_github("scales", ref = "scales-0.2.3-rc")
>   install_github("ggplot2", ref = "ggplot2-0.9.3-rc")
>
> After installation has completed, you will need to restart R. Then you can test your existing code that uses plyr and ggplot2.
>
>
> Installation notes:
>
> This will install plyr from source, which requires that you have a C compiler on your system. Please see this page for information about that (it also describes installing LaTeX, but that's not necessary here):
>
>   http://www.rstudio.com/ide/docs/packages/prerequisites
>
>
> Installing with dev_mode():
>
> Installing the RC versions of these packages is slightly different from usual. Unlike the usual method, these can NOT be installed with the dev_mode() function from devtools, which is normally used to keep development and released packages separate. This is because devtools indirectly depends on plyr and when you load devtools, it will load the version of plyr in your normal library (not your development library). Thus the new version of plyr must be installed NOT in dev_mode(). (If you really require a workaround for this, it is possible; please send an email to the manipulatr mailing list.)
>
>
> If you encounter any problems with the new version, please post to either the ggplot2-dev or manipulatr mailing lists, or file an issue on Github.
>
> Thanks!
> Winston Chang
> Hadley Wickham
>

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I just upgraded from ggplot2 0.9.1 to 0.9.2.1. The way POSIXlt times are mapped to colours has changed, and I don't know how to get back to the old behaviour.

0.9.1:
 The colour scale is a continuous gradient (dark to light blue).
 png : http://ubuntuone.com/1sUwIK5ttAW6wf471g9ZdI

0.9.2/0.9.2.1 <http://0.9.2.1>:
 The colour scale is discretized.
 png : http://ubuntuone.com/7BbACLrxL9oHvsOjF8FBSy

Is there a way to get back the gradient scale in 0.9.2.1? (I did try to search the changelog and the mailing list, to no avail. Pointers to previous discussions would of course be appreciated.)

Here is my code:

library(reshape)
library(ggplot2)

dat <- mutate(data.frame(x=seq(0,10,0.1)),
              y = sin(x),
              t = as.POSIXlt(sprintf("2012-07-18 20:%d:%f", as.integer(x), x)))

summary(dat)

ggplot.version <- sessionInfo("ggplot2")$otherPkgs$ggplot2$Version
cat("this is ggplot2 version", ggplot.version, "\n")

p <- ggplot(dat) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y, color=t))
ggsave(sprintf("time-color-%s.png", ggplot.version))

--
Ronan

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Currently, I have plotted my data using geom_line, geom_smooth and geom_point. However, as you will see the result is suboptimal. A friend of mine helped me to use geom_dotplot instead of geom_point but we both could not solve the problem. Ideally, I would like to have the dots arranged next to each other (group 1, 2, 3, 4 from left to right) and centred on the y-axis at 1-2 or 2-3, respectively. They do not necessarily have to be centred, if this is not possible, but as it is (geom_point and position_dodge) it looks a bit messy. Ideally, I would like to maintain the shapes of the various groups which we did not manage in geom_dotplot. Below, I have pasted in the code which I also attached as an R script. I have also attached the PDFs of a) the original graph which one of the reviewers criticised (…), b) the version using geom_point and position_dodge, and c) a version using geom_dotplot. I would be very grateful if someone could help me with this problem, please.

Best wishes,

Martin

library(ggplot2)

    97.8982300884956, NA, NA, NA, NA, 90.686274509804, 90.4411764705882,
    NA, 97.5510204081633, 93.7414965986395, NA, 88.2820258192651,
    83.8133068520358, NA, 95.6653225806452, 94.6572580645161, NA,
    96.5116279069768, 94.670542635659, NA, 98.2581967213115, 97.438524590164
    ), group = structure(c(2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L,
    1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 4L, 4L,
    4L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 3L, 3L, 3L), .Label = c("carnica EW", "carnica ED",
    "mellifera EW", "mellifera ED"), class = "factor")), .Names = c("trt", "resp",
    "group"), row.names = c(NA, -36L), class = "data.frame")

df.perc.2b <- structure(list(trt = structure(c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L), class = "factor", .Label = c("0-1", "1-2", "2-3")),
    resp = c(NA, 94.0193416337148, 90.4454585871723,
        NA, 97.865467535666, 95.8563947267053),
    group = structure(c(2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L), .Label = c("eggs in worker cells (EW)", "eggs in drone cells (ED)"), class = "factor"),
    se = c(NA, 1.68994661360938, 2.95728999211006,
        NA, 0.549126551165786, 0.824844616926236)),
    .Names = c("trt", "resp", "group", "se"), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame")

    resp = c(100, 94.0193416337148, NA,
        100, 97.865467535666, NA),

ggplot() +

        size = 0.5, colour = "black") +
    geom_smooth(data = df.perc.2b, aes(y = resp, x = trt, group = group, linetype = group, ymax = resp + se,

ggplot() +
    geom_line(data = df.perc.2a, aes(y = resp, x = trt, group = group, linetype = group), stat = "identity",
        size = 0.5, colour = "black") +
    geom_smooth(data = df.perc.2b, aes(y = resp, x = trt, group = group, linetype = group, ymax = resp + se,
        ymin = resp - se), stat = "identity", size = 0.5, colour = "black") +
    geom_dotplot(data = na.omit(df.perc.3), aes(y = resp, x = factor(trt), shape = group, fill = group),
        stackdir = "center", size = 2, stackgroups = TRUE, method = "histodot", binaxis = "y", binpositions = "all") +
    opts(legend.text = theme_text(size = 5), legend.key.size = unit(c(0.9, 0.9), "lines"),
        legend.title = theme_blank())

messages.subject: Re: Problem using shape and fill
messages.body_plain:
On Nov 5, 4:55 pm, Brian Diggs <dig...@ohsu.edu> wrote:
> On 11/5/2012 9:27 AM, Mark wrote:
>
> > I can't find an explanation or work around for a problem I'm having
> > when I use map one variable to shape and another to fill. The below
> > example seems to ignore fill entirely.
>
> > ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg)) +
> >    geom_point(aes(shape=factor(vs), fill=factor(am)), size=4) +
> >    scale_shape_discrete(solid=FALSE)
>
> > This example plots correctly but the legend is incorrect
>
> > ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg)) +
> >    geom_point(aes(shape=factor(vs), fill=factor(am)), size=4) +
> >    scale_shape_manual(values=c(21, 23))
>
> The solid=FALSE argument to scale_shape_discrete does not do what you
> think it does; it selects solid shapes (ones that have the same middle
> color as they are drawn in) rather than fillable shapes (ones which can
> have a different fill color than line color.
>
> For a catalog of all the shapes and the effects of color and fill on
> them, try:
>
> DF <- data.frame(pt = 0:25, x = 1, y = 1)
> ggplot(DF, aes(x=x, y=y, shape=pt)) +
>    geom_point(colour="red", fill="lightblue", size=10) +
>    scale_shape_identity() +
>    facet_wrap(~pt) +
>    theme_bw() +
>    theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
>          axis.title = element_blank(),
>          axis.ticks = element_blank())
>
> Requesting solid shapes (the default) gives 16, 17, 15, 3, 7, and 8.
> Requesting not solid shapes gives 1, 2, 0, 3, 7, 8. Neither set includes
> the fillable ones (21-25), so you have to specify them using a manual
> scale as you do in your second example.
>
> The problem with the legend in the second example is that the shape of
> the points in the legend is, by default, 16. But fill does not have an
> effect of shape 16, so the legend is all black circles. Shape 21 is a
> better choice and that can be specified with
>
> ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg)) +
>    geom_point(aes(shape=factor(vs), fill=factor(am)), size=4) +
>    scale_shape_manual(values=c(21, 23)) +
>    scale_fill_discrete(guide = guide_legend(override.aes = aes(shape = 21)))
>
> --
> Brian S. Diggs, PhD
> Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
> Oregon Health & Science University

Thank you Brian. That helped a lot.

> http://imageshack.us/content_round.php?page=done&l=img194/1445/outrb.png

Since this is not reproducible (we don't have a), some of the following
are just guesses. However, the image was helpful.

>    However, there are a few things that I would like to improve. For example:
>
> 1) Most important: I have 100 years on "x" axis, which is a lot of data,
> and therefore they are squeezed. How can I "stretch" plot dimensions in
> order to display all numbers in a legible way?

year is probably discrete (character or factor) rather than continuous
(numeric). Convert it to numeric and the continuous scale will not make
every value into a tick. If you really need it as a discrete variable,
the breaks option to scale_x_discrete allows you to specify which values
are shown.

> 2) How can I mantain this scale and change only the legend title?

> Options *scale_colour_brewer(palette=5,
> name='Classes') + theme(legend.title=element_text(face = "italic"))* don't
> make any effect.

The aesthetic that corresponds to the legend you see is fill, not
colour. So use scale_fill_brewer, not scale_colour_brewer.

> 3) How can I get rid of that grey bars on the top of the plot?

That is the background of the plot. If you don't want it to be gray, you
can just change that in the theme, or use theme_bw(). If you don't want
the space there at all, then you can set the y axis limits to exactly 0
and 1. You may also need to set expand to c(0,0); I don't recall.

>    Any suggestion?
>
>    Many thanks in advance,
>    Thiago.

messages.subject: Re: plotting geoR variogram
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jean-Baptiste,

There are a couple of problems with geom_line(wls).  Firstly ols and wls are special objects that ggplot knows nothing about, and secondly you are passing them in as the first argument where geom_line expects a mapping.  A general solution for this type of problem is to write a function that takes the special type of object you are interested in as an argument, and outputs a data.frame you can use ggplot to plot.

You know lines(wls) must at some point calculate enough info to draw the line you require, it's just a matter of finding out where.

This first step is too figure out what is happening in lines(ols):
> class(ols)
[1] "variomodel" "variofit"

Tells us ols has class "variomodel", so our best bet is to look at lines.variomodel:

> ?lines.variomodel
> lines.variomodel
function (x, ...)
{
    UseMethod("lines.variomodel")
}
<environment: namespace:geoR>

Not very helpful...looks like lines.variogram is a generic function, we need to figure out which method is being called.

> methods("lines.variomodel")
[1] lines.variomodel.default*     lines.variomodel.grf*
[3] lines.variomodel.krige.bayes* lines.variomodel.likGRF*
[5] lines.variomodel.variofit*

   Non-visible functions are asterisked

Look like lines.variomodel.variofit is our candidate:
getAnywhere("lines.variomodel.variofit")

will spit out the function, and it looks like most of it is calculating the fitted line to be used in the call to the function curve.  One way to get ggplot to plot the fitted line would be to reuse that code but instead of calling curve, outputting a data.frame that ggplot can use.  I put my attempt here: https://gist.github.com/4027851

Source that in and try:
qplot(u,v,data=df_vario) +
 geom_line(aes(x, fit), data = fitted_variofit(ols)) +
 geom_line(aes(x, fit), data = fitted_variofit(wls), linetype = "dashed")

Hope that helps,

Charlotte

messages.subject: Writing plotting functions with the ability to choose by name which columns will be plotted
messages.subject_clean: Writing plotting functions with the ability to choose by name which columns will be plotted
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I'm trying to generate some ggplot functions but give the user the option of choosing which variables to plot by parsing their names (data frame column names).
Seems like a basic option to me to enable function writing but so far I've been unsuccessful -- ggplot either gives an error or otherwise funny results.
For example, given the following minimal data frame:

library(ggplot2)
data2plot <- data.frame(x1 = seq(1,10), y1 = seq(1,10), y2 = seq(10,1))

Now I'd like to generate a ggplot function that will plot a simple scatter plot but will accept column names as input so that the user could choose by name which column to plot.
but...

Running this:

plot.variable <- function(data2plot, y.axis){
 qplot(x1, y = y.axis, data = data2plot)
}
plot.variable(data2plot, y.axis = 'y1')

Plots ten points on the graph with the Y value = 'y1'

Running this:

plot.variable <- function(data2plot, x.axis, y.axis){
  qplot(x = x.axis, y = y.axis, data = data2plot)
}
plot.variable(data2plot, x.axis = 'x1', y.axis = 'y1')

Plots one point 'x1' vs 'y1'

Running this:

plot.variable <- function(data2plot, x.axis, y.axis){
  qplot(data = data2plot, x = data2plot[, x.axis], y = data2plot[, y.axis])
}
plot.variable(data2plot, x.axis = 'x1', y.axis = 'y1')

Actually gives a plot but if I write a function using 'ggplot' instead of qplot:

plot.variable <- function(data2plot, x.axis, y.axis){
  ggplot(data2plot, aes(x = data2plot[, x.axis], y = data2plot[, y.axis])) +
    geom_point()
}
plot.variable(data2plot, x.axis = 'x1', y.axis = 'y1')

Gives and error: 'Error in `[.data.frame`(data2plot, , x.axis) : object 'x.axis' not found'
I could get this function to not give an error if I assign the variables outside the function call (i.e. x.axis <- 'x1', y.axis <- 'y1'), but that causes a mess with more complex functions which include faceting etc. I guess because it doesnt keep the original order of observations as in the data frame. Besides that's obviosly not a solution to my problem.

Is there a solution to this?

Thanks in advance,
Roey

messages.subject: Re: binwidth with freqpoly/histogram and Date or DateTime variable
messages.subject_clean: binwidth with freqpoly/histogram and Date or DateTime variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I'd suggest experimenting with examples that are different enough to expose the default behavior in ggplot2. Here's a small toy example to get you started, using geom_bar() on data that are meant to be interpreted as pre-summarized counts per month:

library('ggplot2')
DF <- data.frame(date = seq(as.Date('2012-01-01'), as.Date('2012-11-01'),
                                by = "months"),
                          val = rpois(11, 50))
ggplot(DF, aes(x = date, y = val)) +
     geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "orange")

You'd use scale_x_date() to modify the format of the dates in the plot if necessary.

The default binwidth in geom_histogram() is range/30 but you can always define your own in a ggplot() or qplot() call by providing a value to the binwidth =  argument; in fact, it's encouraged. There are numerous examples in the on-line help page for geom_histogram(): http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/geom_histogram.html. The binwidth argument also exists in geom_bar(), which I'm assuming you're using with date as the x-variable; see the help page for geom_bar() at the same site for examples.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Plot 3 lines in one graph
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's what I think Ben meant in terms of the toy example (rewritten with cleaner code):

V <- data.frame( time = seq(30), var1 = rnorm(30),
                  var2 = rnorm(30) + 3, var3 = rnorm(30) + 6)
library('reshape2')

# Reshape V from 'wide' form to 'long' form
Vm <- melt(V, id = "time")
str(Vm)
levels(Vm$variable)
head(Vm)

# This form is convenient for ggplot() because now the
# variables Var1-Var3 can be accessed as a single entity:

ggplot(Vm, aes(x = time, y = value, color = variable)) +
    geom_line() +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-2, 8)) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "black"))

You can create a factor on the fly, but it is not immediately obvious how to do so; fortunately, Hadley provided an example in the ggplot2 book. The idea is to put the aesthetic to be created in aes() and sequentially augment its set of values with multiple calls to the geom. You can then use the appropriate scale_* function to fine tune the legend guide.

ggplot(V, aes(x = time)) +
   geom_line(aes(y = var1, color = "var1")) +
   geom_line(aes(y = var2, color = "var2")) +
   geom_line(aes(y = var3, color = "var3")) +
   coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-2, 8)) +
   labs(color = "Variable") +
   scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "black"))

Is that what you were asking about?

Dennis

Thanks for looking at this. I did use geom_bar in fact, not geom_histogram. Using you example, I convinced myself a bit more than binwidth uses days in the case of a Date variable:

library('ggplot2')
DF <- data.frame(date = seq(as.Date('2012-01-01'), as.Date('2012-11-01'),
                                by = "months"),
                          val = rpois(11, 50))

library(scales)
ggplot(DF, aes(x = date)) +
 geom_bar(aes(weight = val),stat = "bin", binwidth = 60, fill = "orange") +scale_x_date(breaks = date_breaks("2 month"),labels = date_format("%b"))

This seems to be putting Jan in bin 1, Feb-Mar in bin 2, etc, though this is not clear from the x-scale.

Maybe I'd be better using something like the following to show the trend, rather than binning as a rough form of smoothing.
ggplot(DF, aes(x = date,y = val)) +
 geom_point()  + geom_path() + geom_smooth()

It's not what I wanted though and I'd really like to understand binwidth better. Maybe I'd have to look at the source code. None of the examples seem to use a Date or DateTime variable.

Hywel
@hywelm

On Thursday, November 8, 2012 9:40:42 PM UTC, Dennis Murphy wrote:
> Hi:
>
> I'd suggest experimenting with examples that are different enough to expose the default behavior in ggplot2. Here's a small toy example to get you started, using geom_bar() on data that are meant to be interpreted as pre-summarized counts per month:
>
> library('ggplot2')
> DF <- data.frame(date = seq(as.Date('2012-01-01'), as.Date('2012-11-01'),
>                                 by = "months"),
>                           val = rpois(11, 50))
> ggplot(DF, aes(x = date, y = val)) +
>      geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "orange")
>
> You'd use scale_x_date() to modify the format of the dates in the plot if necessary.
>
> The default binwidth in geom_histogram() is range/30 but you can always define your own in a ggplot() or qplot() call by providing a value to the binwidth =  argument; in fact, it's encouraged. There are numerous examples in the on-line help page for geom_histogram(): http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/geom_histogram.html. The binwidth argument also exists in geom_bar(), which I'm assuming you're using with date as the x-variable; see the help page for geom_bar() at the same site for examples.
>
> Dennis

messages.body_plain:
I'm pretty confused as to what you're trying to do. mtcars is a data
frame, and ggplot works best with data frames, so why are you using
llply? In any event, you're operating on columns 9:11 of mtcars, which
doesn't include the 'cyl' column, which is a problem right there.

Personally, to plot multiple columns I'd do something like this:

library( reshape )
mtcars1 <- mtcars[ c( 2, 9:11 ) ]
mtcars1 <- melt( mtcars, id.vars="cyl" )
ggplot( mtcars1, aes( cyl, value ) ) + geom_boxplot() + facet_grid(
variable~., scales="free_y" )

Ben

Am Montag, 5. November 2012 18:57:02 UTC+1 schrieb winston:
> Hi everyone -
>
> (We've bcc'd everyone who's a maintainer of a package that depends, imports or suggests ggplot2 or plyr.)
>
> We have prepared release candidates (RCs) for plyr 1.8 and ggplot2 0.9.3, which we plan to release to CRAN simultaneously. Unless there are major unexpected bugs, they will be in the RC phase for a about a month before they are sent to CRAN on December 1.
>
> The purpose of the RC phase is to uncover unexpected bugs in ggplot2 and plyr. These releases do not include any changes that we expect to break existing code, but we hope that this period will allows to uncover any unexpected changes and remedying them before releasing to CRAN. The next version of ggplot2 (0.9.3) contains primarily bugfixes, while the next version of plyr (1.8) has a number of new features and performance enhancements. For the full list of changes, see:
>
>   https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/master/NEWS
>   https://github.com/hadley/plyr/blob/master/NEWS
>
> It would be very helpful if you could try out the RC version and see if it breaks any of your existing code.  To try out the the new versions, run the following code:
>
>   install.packages("devtools")
>   library(devtools)
>   install_github("plyr", ref = "plyr-1.8-rc")
>   install_github("gtable", ref = "gtable-0.1.2-rc")
>   install_github("scales", ref = "scales-0.2.3-rc")
>   install_github("ggplot2", ref = "ggplot2-0.9.3-rc")
>
> After installation has completed, you will need to restart R. Then you can test your existing code that uses plyr and ggplot2.
>
>
> Installation notes:
>
> This will install plyr from source, which requires that you have a C compiler on your system. Please see this page for information about that (it also describes installing LaTeX, but that's not necessary here):
>
>   http://www.rstudio.com/ide/docs/packages/prerequisites
>
>
> Installing with dev_mode():
>
> Installing the RC versions of these packages is slightly different from usual. Unlike the usual method, these can NOT be installed with the dev_mode() function from devtools, which is normally used to keep development and released packages separate. This is because devtools indirectly depends on plyr and when you load devtools, it will load the version of plyr in your normal library (not your development library). Thus the new version of plyr must be installed NOT in dev_mode(). (If you really require a workaround for this, it is possible; please send an email to the manipulatr mailing list.)
>
>
> If you encounter any problems with the new version, please post to either the ggplot2-dev or manipulatr mailing lists, or file an issue on Github.
>
> Thanks!
> Winston Chang
> Hadley Wickham
>

messages.subject: Re: Latex type labels?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This isn't a perfect representation of your graph and its requirements, but here's how you define expressions as labels in a legend guide and pass them into a ggplot() call.

# Create a list of expressions of the same length as
# the number of unique levels in variable
varexp <- list(expression(alpha + beta*x), expression(gamma + delta*x),
                expression(zeta + theta*x))

# Since y is passed in as the input data frame, you don't need
# to say y$value, y$variable, y$"epsilon_h" in ggplot()
ggplot(y, aes(x = epsilon_h, y = value, color = variable)) +
    geom_point(shape = 1) +
    scale_color_manual(breaks = levels(y$variable),
                       values = c("blue", "red", "green"),
                       labels = varexp) +
    geom_smooth(method = lm, aes(linetype = variable), se = FALSE, fullrange = TRUE, size = 1.5) +
    labs(x = expression(epsilon[h]), y = "value") +
    xlim(-5000, -100) +
    scale_linetype_manual(breaks = levels(y$variable),
                          values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotdash"),
                          labels = varexp) +
    theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 12))

I tried using scale_color_hue() with leading arguments breaks, values and labels, but it returned an error:
Error in discrete_scale("colour", "hue", hue_pal(h, c, l, h.start, direction),  :
  unused argument(s) (values = c("blue", "red", "green"))

According to the help page, scale_*_hue() is supposed to be able to take such arguments at the beginning of the call and pass them to discrete_scale(), but I couldn't get that to work. Instead, I used scale_color_manual() and scale_linetype_manual()  above. To darken the color hues, it appears that you'll need to find the hex values of the colors you want and substitute them for c("red", "blue", "green") in the values argument of scale_color_manual(). ggplot2 will not let you construct multiple legends for the same aesthetic.

On the off chance that you were not aware of this fact, if you want to merge two scales into one, they need to have the same breaks and labels, which is why varexp is passed as the value of the labels = argument in both legends.

Dennis

Hi:

On Sun, Nov 11, 2012 at 4:39 PM, Ignacio Martinez <igna...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thanks a lot Dennis!
>
> Just 2 more questions:
> 1. How can I have a formula instead of "variable" as the title of the legends?

Use the labs() function and write an expression as the value of both color and linetype; you need to make the same title for both if the legends are to be merged (i.e., you really need the legend title, breaks and labels to be the same in a merged legend...which of course occurred to me about five seconds after sending my previous reply...)

> 2. How can I write f(cdot) where cdot is a centered dot?

R uses plotmath() for mathematical symbols in expressions, and AFAICT there is no function to render a single centered dot in an expression, although there is a cdots function that generates a raised ellipsis for sums, products and the like. See ?plotmath for the symbols and operators it supports.

D.

messages.subject: Re: add species labels using geom_text
messages.body_plain:
Heather,

Working backwards through your questions: qplot is just a convenient
wrapper for ggplot and its related functions. I use it frequently for
quick looks at things, but to build up a complex plot, you'll probably
want to use ggplot.

In your example, you're pulling data out of the data frame to plot it.
Don't! Keeping things in a single df makes things easier.

I think you want to do something like this:

qplot(rank,logabun,data=sp52,label=species,geom=c("text"))

Here, you're telling qplot to plot rank (x) versus logabun (y), with
labels pulled from species, and use geom_text. If you wanted to have
points as well as lines, you'd change that last part to
geom=c("point","text"). Alternatively, using ggplot:

ggplot( sp52, aes( rank, logabun ) ) + geom_text( aes( label=species ) )

Hope this is useful,
Ben

messages.subject: hysteresis plot
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

It may be a very simple question,….but how I can create a hyterisis plot (counter clockwise), for example, drug effect (PD) is observed later (=delayed) than the actual drug concentration (PK), and when PK vs. PD is plotted with line, it shows hysteresis.

Here is a small, toy example. I can create a hyterisis plot with xyplot, but the line is connected with the order of x-variable with ggplot so can’t produce what I want (I want to connect the line with the order of TIME)…..I tried reorder, relevel, but it doesn’t work (or maybe I am doing wrong).

Could anybody help me?

Kaori

#example data

d <- data.frame(ID=rep(1:2, each=10), TIME=rep(c(0,0.5,1,2,4,6,8,12,16,24),2),

          PK=c(0,2,6,20,50,40,20,10,5,3,0,1,3,12,30,35,20,5,4,1),

          PD=c(100,102,105,110,120,130,160,150,140,135,60,65,70,75,80,95,100,90,85,70))

library(lattice)

xyplot(PD~PK, data=d, type="b", group=ID)

library(ggplot2)

d$ID <- as.factor(d$ID)

ggplot(d, aes(x= PK, y=PD, group=ID, colour=ID)) + geom_line()

messages.subject: Two datasets with two legends?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I am plotting a dataset and adding geom_vline from a second dataset to mark certain actions in time. However, I was unable to find out how to get the legends related to geom_vline and the second dataset.

I'm using something similar to that, execpt that I'm using time as x axis. I would like to have at least a legend with "Action" in the "y2" dataset. Should I include y2 in a melted y1?

Thank you all!

guillaume

-

y1 = data.frame(A = c(1:100), B = rnorm(100), C = rnorm(100), D = rnorm(100))
y1.m = melt(y1, id="A")

y2 = data.frame(.A. = c(10, 50, 80), Press = c(NA, 2 , 3), Action = c(".a.",".b.",".c."))

p = ggplot(y1.m , aes(x=A, y=value, color=variable)) +
         geom_vline(data=y2, aes(xintercept=.A., linetype=Action, alpha=Press)) +
         geom_point() +
         facet_grid(variable ~ ., scale="free_y")
p

Since you are using qplot syntax, I don't think facet_wrap knows where
to look for the GROUP variable. In fact, I am surprised that that even
worked anyway; did you have an attach(DATA) somewhere?  You would be
better off switching to ggplot syntax and using an explicit data argument.

ggplot(DATA, aes(x = WEEK, y = MEAN, colour = Location)) +
   geom_point() +
   geom_line() +
   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = MEAN-SD, ymax = MEAN+SD), width = 0.2) +
   facet_wrap(~ GROUP, scales = "free", nrow = 5, ncol = 2) +
   xlab("Week") +

messages.subject_clean: Would like a new geom to replace geom_bar(aes(x, y))
messages.body_plain:
Since according to:

* `stat_bin` now produces warning messages when it is used with set or
  mapped y values. Previously, it was possible to use `stat_bin` and
  also set/map y values; if there was one y value per group, it would
  display the y values from the data, instead of the counts of cases for
  each group. This usage is deprecated and will be removed in a future
  version of ggplot2. (Winston Chang. Fixes #632)

it will be necessary in the future to specify stat = "identity" when using the y aesthetic in geom_bar how about giving us a new geom that defaults to stat = "identity" for convenience.  It will otherwise be a new nuisance always having to specify stat = "identity" in those cases.  Perhaps something like:

     geom_bary <- function(..., stat = "identity") geom_bar(..., stat = stat)

messages.subject: Re: ggplot issue with axes labels
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jefe,

If you have too many labels, don't print them all:

 p + scale_x_continuous("", breaks=c(1, 3),
        labels = as.Date(c("2010-06-03", "2010-06-07")))

you can also angle them to make more room:

 p + scale_x_continuous("", breaks=c(1, 3),
        labels = as.Date(c("2010-06-03", "2010-06-07"))) +
  theme(axis.text=element_text(angle = 70, hjust=1))

Best,
Ista

df <- data.frame(x=1:5,y=1:5)

everything in a single data frame so you can do something like
+geom_point( aes( color=treatment ) ).

messages.subject: Re: extend nonlinear regression lines
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's one way you could do it, following the hint shown in Kohske's blog post:

DF <- data.frame(x = runif(30, -5, -1), y = runif(30, 0, 3))
DF2 <- data.frame(x = seq(-10, 0, by = 0.1))

ggplot(DF, aes(x = x)) +
    geom_point(aes(y = y)) +
    stat_function(data = DF2, aes(x = x),
                  fun = function(x) 2.7223 * exp(0.21834 * x), color = "blue") +
    stat_function(data = DF2, aes(x = x),
                  fun = function(x) 1.3203 * exp(0.21978 * x), color = "red") +
    stat_function(data = DF2, aes(x = x),
                  fun = function(x) 2.7071 * exp(0.2001 * x), color = "orange")

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
The script below draws a polygon over a world map. It’s reproducible – you should be able to copy/paste to see how this is done. Using over() from the sp package, I can then easily find the number of points which lie in each polygon drawn.

coordsX = c(76.7864778,  -3.1111604,   1.0029375, 109.7523700,  79.0270900,  18.2920100,  -5.0525788,  -9.4254852,   0.1314163,
34.9690523)
coordsY = c(13.8176899, -32.7283195,  12.9977900,   0.4631664,  25.1343479,  13.8666859,  57.5056500,  53.8051547,  54.7481300,
57.7765223)
myCoords = data.frame(coordsX,coordsY)

library(sp)
coordinates(myCoords) <- c('coordsX', 'coordsY')
plot(myCoords)
crs.geo <- CRS("+proj=longlat +ellps=WGS84 +datum=WGS84") # define projection
proj4string(myCoords) <- crs.geo
plot(myCoords, pch=20, col="steelblue")

library(maptools)
data(wrld_simpl)
plot(wrld_simpl, add=T)

library(dismo)
mypolygon <- drawPoly()    # click on the map to draw a polygon and press ESC
proj4string(mypolygon) <- crs.geo

My question  is – can I draw polygons in the same way using a function in the ggmap package?

messages.subject: Re: Stat smooth
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Another way to do this is to remove the color aesthetic from the ggplot() call and move it to geom_point() instead:

ggplot(mtcars,aes(x=disp,y=mpg)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = as.factor(cyl))) +
    geom_smooth(method = lm)

Placing the color aesthetic in the ggplot() call means that it will be expected to be present in *all* subsequent layers, which forces one to use group = 1 as an aesthetic in geom_smooth() to override the expectation of separate lines by levels of the color aesthetic.

Both methods are instructive and worth understanding: e.g., if I had multiple layers in a ggplot, most of which used color (say, for example, colored boxplots and points) then I'd probably put the color aesthetic in ggplot() and use the group = 1 device for geom_smooth() as Ben showed. OTOH, if I only wanted color in one or two layers of a multi-layer ggplot, I would declare them as aesthetics in the geom(s) of interest and not in ggplot(), as in my code above.

Dennis

  geom_vline(data = y2, aes(xintercept = A, linetype = Action)) +

  geom_point(aes(y = value, color = variable)) +
  facet_grid(variable ~ ., scale = "free_y")

  geom_vline(data = y2, aes(xintercept = A, color = Action)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = value, linetype = variable)) +

> dev.off()

Hi guys,

It really is a good idea to read the docs:

?geom_vline

Arguments:
show_guide: should a legend be drawn? (defaults to ‘FALSE’)

So we need

ggplot(y1.m , aes(x=A, y=value, color=variable)) +
  geom_vline(data=y2, aes(xintercept=.A., linetype=Action,

alpha=Press), show_guide=TRUE) +

  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(variable ~ ., scale="free_y")

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: Re: Plotting Distributions with Density plots
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for sending the data, Sarita. You're right, there are no values
<0...but you're applying an xlim, I see, which probably isn't doing
what you want. That's tossing out data not in the (-1,1) range;
compare to

> ggplot(z, aes(x=value, fill=variable)) + geom_density(alpha=0.9) + coord_cartesian(xlim=c(-1,1))

So: yes, there's definitely an artifact (negative x values) being
produced when an xlim is applied; I don't know if this is an expected
consequence of the stat_density algorithm, or a quirk in the
geom_density display code. But you probably want to be using
coord_cartesian, which works fine. If you *do* want to subset your
data, I'd do it before the call to ggplot in this case.

Hope this is useful,

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Problem with boxcox_trans
messages.body_plain:
But wouldn't it make more sense to return the transformation object itself rather than the function that returns the transformation object? Otherwise you are force to treat 0 differently.

What I'm suggesting is that boxcox_trans should be something like this

boxcox_trans <- function(p){
    if (abs(p) < 1e-07)
        return(log_trans()) # changed from return(log_trans)
    trans <- function(x) (x^p - 1)/p * sign(x - 1)
    inv <- function(x) (abs(x) * p + 1 * sign(x))^(1/p)
    trans_new(str_c("pow-", format(p)), trans, inv)
}

messages.subject: Re: Drawing order on stat_density2d and stat_contour obscures some layers.
messages.subject_clean: Drawing order on stat_density2d and stat_contour obscures some layers.
messages.body_plain:
> I am having the problem that when adding stat_contour or stat_density2d
> the "upper" layer polygons are being obscured by lower ones.

Well, yes, later filled polygons will obscure previous ones. This is because ggplot2, like grid, operates on a "painter's model" of graphics (new overwrites old at any given location). The order in which layers are drawn can sometimes matter. Alpha transparency can be used to mitigate the problem. Try various fixed values of alpha (assuming the geom supports it) and use the one that looks the best to you.

Example:

data(geyser, "MASS")
(m <- ggplot(geyser, aes(x = duration, y = waiting)) +
   geom_point() + xlim(0.5, 6) + ylim(40, 110))
m + stat_density2d(aes(fill = ..level..), geom="polygon")
m + stat_density2d(aes(fill = ..level..), geom="polygon", alpha = 0.2)

The colorbar issue is a side point that can be handled separately using guides().

A more mundane example of the painter's model:

DF <- data.frame(x = seq(10), y = seq(10))
# line overwrites points
ggplot(DF, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point(size = 3, color = "orange") +
     geom_line()
# points overwrite line
ggplot(DF, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_line() +
     geom_point(size = 3, color = "orange")
# compromise
ggplot(DF, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_line() +
     geom_point(size = 3, color = "orange", alpha = 0.6)

Dennis

The problem is that qplot draws the plot with the geom_point default geom, and then you are adding your geom_dotplot. So the points are being drawn twice.  I would suggest using ggplot() rather than qplot(), so the only time they are drawn is when you explicitly add the dotplot layer eg

ggplot(data=tt, aes(x=pathway,y=fc)) + geom_dotplot(binaxis="y", aes(fill=factor(de)), colour=NA, binwidth=0.01,binstataxis="y")

cheers

two plots are different. Does anybody have the ggplot code that can
reproduce the "plot" result? Thanks!

library(ggplot2)

png('main2.png')
qplot(x, y, data=dfr)+stat_smooth(method='loess', span=.8)+ylim(0,100)
dev.off()

messages.body_plain:
The problem is that ylim() will drop all the data points outside the range, and then the loess gets calculated on that. To avoid this, use coord_cartesian instead:

x <-1:100
dfr <-data.frame(x, y=x+rnorm(100,0,100))
qplot(x, y, data=dfr) + stat_smooth(method='loess', span=.8) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,100))

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This is a little extreme, but here's a toy example. Basically, you need to reduce the legend.key.height theme element.

 DF <- data.frame(gp = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:3], each = 20)),
                   x = seq(20),
                   y = 0.5 + rep(0:2, each = 20) +
                             0.3 * rep(seq(20), 3) + rnorm(60))
library('ggplot2')
library('grid')   # needed for the unit() function call below

ggplot(DF, aes(x, y, color = gp)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE) +
    theme(legend.position = c(0.15, 0.82),
              legend.key.height = unit(0.5, "mm"))

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Transparent Theme
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

The theming system was changed in version 0.9.2. The primary changes are:
   (i) use theme() instead of opts()
   (ii) use element_*() instead of theme_*().
The new system also has relative sizing and inheritance, which is reflected in the modification to your theme function below. I've edited this as a complete theme function since it defines all of the individual theme elements.

theme_transparent <- function (base_size = 12, base_family = "Helvetica"){
    theme(
    line = element_line(colour = "black", size = 0.5, linetype = 1, lineend = "butt"),
    rect = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = "black", size = 0.5, linetype = 1),
    text = element_text(family = base_family, face = "plain",
                        colour = "black", size = base_size,
                        hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0.5, angle = 0, lineheight = 0.9),
    axis.line = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), colour = 'white', vjust = 1),
    axis.ticks = element_line(colour = "white", size = 0.2),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = 'white', vjust = 1),
    axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5),
    axis.ticks.length = unit(0.3, "lines"),
    axis.ticks.margin = unit(0.5, "lines"),
    legend.background = element_rect(colour = NA),
    legend.key = element_rect(colour = "white", fill = 'transparent'),
    legend.key.size = unit(1.2, "lines"),
    legend.key.height = NULL,
    legend.key.width = NULL,
    legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), colour = 'white'),
    legend.title = element_text(size = rel(0.8), face = "bold", hjust = 0, colour = 'white'),
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.text.align = NULL,
    legend.title.align = NULL,
    legend.direction = "vertical",
    legend.box = NULL,
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
    panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = "white"),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey20", size = 0.2),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(colour = "grey5", size = 0.5),
    panel.margin = unit(0.25, "lines"),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey30", colour = "grey10"),
    strip.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), colour = 'white'),
    strip.text.y = element_text(angle = -90),
    plot.background = element_rect(colour = 'NA', fill = 'transparent'),
    plot.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.2),
    plot.margin = unit(c(1, 1, 0.5, 0.5), "lines"),

    complete = TRUE)   # denotes that this is a complete theme function
 }

# Verify that this is a complete theme function:
attr(theme_transparent(), "complete")

# Example of use:
qplot(1:10, 1:10, geom = "point", colour = I("blue")) + theme_transparent()

I don't know whether that's what you wanted or not, but it's what my naive transcription of your theme function to the new system produced. If this is not what you expected, perhaps you could post a graphic from the old system that used your theme function.

It's quite possible in the new system to take a built-in theme like theme_bw() and use the %+replace% operator to replace the values of certain theme elements. For example, this looks rather similar to David Kahle's theme_nothing() with the exception that you retain the axis grids. Here's the revised theme_nothing() in the new system, which replaces the values of certain elements in theme_bw():

theme_nothing <- function(base_size = 12, base_family = "Helvetica") { theme_bw(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) %+replace% theme( rect = element_blank(), line = element_blank(), text = element_blank(), axis.ticks.length = unit(0.01, "cm"), axis.ticks.margin = unit(0, "lines") ) }

Example:

qplot(1:10, 1:10, geom = "point", colour = I("blue")) + theme_nothing()

The axis.tick.* values are different from yours and you would need a non-blank set of axis element values, but this is the general idea.

You need ggplot2-0.9.2 or later in order for this code to work.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: plotting polynomials
messages.body_plain:
What I usually do is calculate the upper and lower bounds of CI and pass those values to geom_smooth. Something along the lines of

...
geom_smooth(model.pred, aes(ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl, fill = habituation, colour = habituation),
            stat = "identity", alpha = 0.1) +
...

where ymin and ymax represent the aforementioned bounds. Fill and colour are there for making things pretty and stat should be set to "identity" to tell ggplot2 to not bother calculating anything but to take your values. Alpha is set to something rather transparent. model.pred is the data.frame with (at least) columns lcl and ucl.

Cheers,
Roman

messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody,
    did anyone have experience plotting the results of the mixed/multilevel models as produced by lmer?

the output of the lmer, like
time
model<- lmer(outcome~1+time+(1+| subjectID))

would be a S4 object ( not clear what that it and the documentation left my rookie mind confused).
Does anyone know of an easy way to graphs the results of this model in ggplot2 by extracting the necessary parameters from the 4S output from lmer?
For example, if I have 1000 subjects in the longitudinal model above, i would have 1000 individual trajectories could be showed by

coef(model)

function. So, ideally it would produce 1000 lines to go on the plot.The

fixef(model)

would spit out the parameters for the overall trajectory ( intercept + slope), which could be over-imposed over the multiple lines plots from (coef(model)).
but the trick is to extract those parameters from the 4S lmer objects. To resume` the an opening question:

Does anyone know of an easy way use  4S object from lmer to create plots with ggplot2?

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to transform the x axis, so that instead of getting, say:
0, 50, 100, 150, 200

the labels appear with a transformation that depends on 'x', and on another
attribute of the dataframe (say, attribute(df)$myattribute), such that the
final result is x * myattribute

I can create a function to change the labels:
-----8<---------------
myformat <- function(x) return(x * attributes(df)$myattribute
-----8<---------------

But my problem is that this can't be done inside a function that, as an
argument, has the dataframe:
-----8<---------------
f <- function(df) {
  # Some calculations
  # ...
  ggplot(df, ....) + scale_x_continuous(labels=myformat)
}
-----8<---------------

So the question is how can I pass a secondary argument to
'scale_x_continuous' that refers to an attribute of the original dataframe?

I have tried several approaches with no luck, including a double function:
-----8<---------------
myformat <- function() {
  function(x) return(x * attributes(df)$myattribute
}
# And then inside the f function:
  ggplot(df, ....) + scale_x_continuous(labels=myformat())
-----8<---------------

And passing all arguments, but then 'x' is not found:
-----8<---------------
myformat <- function(x, a) return(x * a)
  ggplot(df, ....) + scale_x_continuous(labels=myformat(x, a=attributes(df)$myattribute))
-----8<---------------

Thank you,
--
-  Xavier  -

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 for plotting lmer output
messages.body_plain:
Hey Andrey, It was good seeing you at that conference thingy the other week.  Great work, by the way.  You have good instincts about pulling the values out of the 'S4' object.  There are a bunch of differences between S3 and S4, but for the purposes of this, the only practical difference is that you use a '@' to pull out values from the `mer` object, instead of using a '$'.

There's no native way to specify a lmer model to ggplot2's `stat_smooth` function, as far as I know.  I imagine it's because there are so many ways to specify a MLM.  Instead, my recommendation is to pull out the predicted/modeled values from the `mer` object (which is returned by lmer).  This occurs below where `dsPredict` is defined.

I just realized I used a different capitalization scheme for the variables, so be careful with that, I guess.  If I left out some important details, please tell me.

rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))
library(ggplot2)
library(plyr)
library(lme4)

subjectCount <- 20
timePointCount <- 11

populationIntercept <- 1
populationSlope <- 2.5
subjectIntercept <- rnorm(subjectCount)
subjectSlope <- rnorm(subjectCount)
dsFull <- data.frame(
  SubjectID=factor(rep(seq_len(subjectCount), each=timePointCount)),
  Time=rep(seq_len(timePointCount), times=subjectCount),
  G0=populationIntercept,
  G1=populationSlope,
  B0=rep(subjectIntercept, each=timePointCount),
  B1=rep(subjectSlope, each=timePointCount),
  E=rnorm(subjectCount*timePointCount),
  Y=NA_real_
)

dsFull$Y <- (dsFull$G0 + dsFull$B0) + (dsFull$G1 + dsFull$B1) * dsFull$Time + dsFull$E
ds <- dsFull[, c("SubjectID", "Time", "Y")]
# m1 <- lmer(Y ~ 1 + Time + (1 | SubjectID), data=ds)
m2 <- lmer(Y ~ 1 + Time + (1 + Time | SubjectID), data=ds)

dsPredict <- data.frame(
  m2@flist,  #The grouping factors for the random effects

messages.subject: Re: plotting list object using ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's one attempt; note that the ggplot() function generally takes
data frames as input, so the data manipulation game is to produce a
data frame out of the vectors of simulated success proportions. It is
then 'melted' using the reshape2 package and the melted data frame is
passed to ggplot(). The purpose of melting is to create a factor
variable whose levels are the sample size strings, since they are the
labels you want for the facets in facet_wrap() below.

N <- 8619170
nn <- c(1000, 1200, 3000)
p <- .27
nsim <- 100

# This works because a data frame is a special case of a list object
DF <- data.frame(lapply(nn, function(n) rhyper(nsim, N * p, N * (1 - p), n)/n))
names(DF) <- paste("n =", nn)

library(reshape2)
library(ggplot2)
DFm <- melt(DF)

ggplot(DFm, aes(x = value)) +
     geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.001) +
     theme_bw() +
     geom_vline(xintercept = 0.27, color = "red", linetype = "longdash") +
     facet_wrap(~ variable, ncol = 1) +
     labs(x = "Success proportion", y = "Frequency")

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Problem with boxcox_trans
messages.body_plain:
Judging by Dianne Cook's response and another response that apparently
didn't get posted to the group, I think my concern is misunderstood.
I understand that a Box-Cox Transformation with p=0 is defined as the
log transformation, but I believe it is a bug that the function
boxcox_trans(p=0) returns an object of class "function" (the log_trans
function) and not an object with class "trans" as all of the other
*_trans functions and boxcox_trans with any other values of p do.

> class(log_trans(base=10))
[1] "trans"
> class(log_trans())
[1] "trans"
> class(logit_trans())
[1] "trans"
> class(atanh_trans())
[1] "trans"
> class(boxcox_trans(p=0.5))
[1] "trans"
> class(boxcox_trans(p=0))
[1] "function"

It seems that rather than return log_trans boxcox_trans should return
log_trans(base=exp(1)).

Mark Lyman

On Nov 20, 9:27 am, Mark <mark.ly...@gmail.com> wrote:
> But wouldn't it make more sense to return the transformation object
> itself rather than the function that returns the transformation object?
> Otherwise you are force to treat 0 differently.
>
> What I'm suggesting is that boxcox_trans should be something like this
>
> boxcox_trans <- function(p){
>
>     if (abs(p) < 1e-07)
>         return(log_trans()) # changed from return(log_trans)
>     trans <- function(x) (x^p - 1)/p * sign(x - 1)
>     inv <- function(x) (abs(x) * p + 1 * sign(x))^(1/p)
>     trans_new(str_c("pow-", format(p)), trans, inv)
>
>
>
> }
> On Tuesday, November 20, 2012 9:13:16 AM UTC-7, Di wrote:

>

>
> > cheers,

> > than return a transformation it returns the function log_trans.
>

> > > boxcox_trans(p=0)function (base = exp(1))

> > {

> >     inv <- function(x) base^x

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's one approach to what I think you want:

# Convert the matrices to data frames, create some
# new variables and row concatenate the results
resDF <- ldply(lapply(paste0("res", 1:3), function(x) {
                      d <- as.data.frame(get(x))
                      d$category <- rownames(d)
                      rownames(d) <- NULL
                      d$set <- substring(x, 4, 4)
                      d  }  ), rbind)

# Plot
ggplot(resDF, aes(x = category, y = mean, color = set)) +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = low, ymax = upper),
                    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
    labs(y = "Effect", x = "") +
    coord_flip() +
    ggtitle("Fixed effects estimates from the main model") +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "orange", "forestgreen"))

There appears to be a relationship between the size of the effect and
the length of the pointrange; you may want to check into that further.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: migrate theme to 0.9.2.1
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Is this what you wanted? This should work for version 0.9.2 +. Some comments:

(1) modifyList() is no longer supported in the new theming system; use
the %+replace% operator instead.
(2) I added fill = NA to panel.border's properties because without it,
the fill color overwrites the graphics panel region and you get what
looks like an empty plotting region (although it really isn't).
(3) Notice how the element properties are modified inside theme()
rather than list(). This is consistent with the notion of replacing
specific element properties of theme_bw().
(4) The new theming system supports inheritance of properties, so it
is now only necessary to specify axis.text rather than both
axis.text.x and axis.text.y; they both inherit the property size = 15
from axis.text. Since there was only one common property in
axis.title.x and axis.title.y, I left them alone.

theme_boxplot2 <- function(base_size = 12)
{
       theme_bw(base_size) %+replace%
             theme(legend.key.size=unit(15,"points"),
                  legend.text=element_text(size=I(13)),
                  legend.key=element_blank(),
                  legend.title=element_blank(),
                  legend.position="none",
                  plot.margin=unit(c(0.25,2,0.25,2), "lines"),
                  panel.border=element_rect(colour='black', fill = NA),
                  panel.margin=unit(0,"lines"),
                  axis.ticks.length=unit(1,"mm"),
                  axis.ticks.margin = unit(0, "lines"),
                  axis.text=element_text(size=15),
                  axis.title.x=element_text(hjust=.55, vjust=-.01, size=17),
                  axis.title.y=element_text(size=17, angle=90,
hjust=.56, vjust=-.001),
                  panel.grid.major=element_blank(),
                  panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),
                  strip.text.x=element_text(size=14),
                  strip.background=element_rect(colour='black', fill='white')
                  )
}

ggplot(data=cars, aes(x=factor(speed), y=dist)) + geom_boxplot() +
                      xlab("speed") + ylab("distance") + theme_boxplot2()

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: scale_shape question
messages.body_plain:
Revisiting this one because I realized there was a problem with the legend. In the code I supplied previously, the legend for fill used the default point shape, 16. This point shape only usees 'colour' and not 'fill', and so both points in the legend are black.

Here's a fixed version. It uses guide_legend to specify the shape used in the legend. (I also changed the shapes to make them easier to distinguish.)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg)) +
    geom_point(aes(shape=factor(vs), fill=factor(am))) +

    scale_shape_manual(values=c(21, 24)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values=c(NA, "black"),
        guide=guide_legend(override.aes=list(shape=21)))

-Winston

messages.subject: Plotting Regression Discontinuity
messages.body_plain:
In plotting regression discontinuity I would like to extrapolate the line for the treatment group forward beyond the cut point and the line for the control group backward beyond the cut point, both with a different line type that changes when the fit line reaches the cut point. In the examples below 20 is the cut point. I would like for the red line to change line type moving to the right once it passes the cut point (i.e. from solid to dashed) and the same thing to occur when the blue line passes the cut point going left. I have no idea how to do this or if it's possible.

Thanks for your assistance.

## Example

prtst<-c(3,4,7,8,9,12,15,17,18,19,7,5,10,12,16,17,15,4,9,16,22,40,30,24,25,32,53,68,29,32,24,52,69,34,55,47,33,34,37,60,58,52,50,44,44)

prtstT<-ifelse(prtst<=20,0,1)
prtst2<-prtst-21

m1<-lm(pstst~prtst2*prtstT)
summary(m1)

data <- data.frame(prtst = prtst, pstst = pstst, prtstT = prtstT, prtst2 = prtst2)

ggplot(data, aes(x = prtst, y = pstst)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(data = subset(data, prtstT == 0), aes(prtst, pstst), method = "lm",
                          se = F, colour = "red", size = 1) +   ## Treatment group
  geom_smooth(data = subset(data, prtstT == 1), aes(prtst, pstst), method = "lm",
                           se = F, colour = "blue", size = 1) +   ## Control group
  geom_vline(x = 20, size = 1) +
  ggtitle("Regression Discontinuity Example w/o Fullrange")

                          se = F, colour = "red", size = 1, fullrange = T) +
  geom_smooth(data = subset(data, prtstT == 1), aes(prtst, pstst), method = "lm",
                          se = F, colour = "blue", size = 1, fullrange = T) +

> Hi:

> Is this what you wanted? This should work for version 0.9.2 +. Some comments:
>
> (1) modifyList() is no longer supported in the new theming system; use
> the %+replace% operator instead.
> (2) I added fill = NA to panel.border's properties because without it,
> the fill color overwrites the graphics panel region and you get what
> looks like an empty plotting region (although it really isn't).
> (3) Notice how the element properties are modified inside theme()
> rather than list(). This is consistent with the notion of replacing
> specific element properties of theme_bw().
> (4) The new theming system supports inheritance of properties, so it
> is now only necessary to specify axis.text rather than both
> axis.text.x and axis.text.y; they both inherit the property size = 15
> from axis.text. Since there was only one common property in
> axis.title.x and axis.title.y, I left them alone.
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

After looking at Josh's nicely done example at the UCLA site, I made a
couple of changes to your code; in particular, your bandwidth needs to
be reduced because the response ranges from 0 to 1. If you set the
bandwidth to 1, you'll only get one or two histogram bars and it's
pointless to draw a density plot over it.

p <- ggplot(TobitTimeH3, aes(x = PctWeakTies, fill = factor(NR_score)))
p + stat_bin(binwidth = 0.1) +

     stat_function(fun = f, size = 1,

              args = list(var = TobitTimeH3$PctWeakTies, bw = 0.1))

NR_score was converted to a factor; once that was done, the error
message disappeared. However, I wonder about the purpose of using 12
distinct fill colors in a single histogram. Perhaps some form of
aggregation of scores is in order (see the cut() function).

Dennis

d <- qplot(qsec, mpg, data=mtcars, colour=as.character(cyl),
shape=as.character(gear))

Hi Dennis,

That worked, thanks a lot!

It helped knowing how to cut date objects too, using:

Thank you wonderful ggplot2 community,

Dhaval

> Hi:
>
> Here's a toy example to illustrate:
>
> DF <- data.frame(x = x, y = intercpt + slope*x + rnorm(100, s = 2),
>                   region = cut(x, c(0, 30, 60, 100)))
> ggplot(DF, aes(x = x, y = y, color = region)) +
>     geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = lm, size = 1)
>
> If you'd like different labels for the legend key items, look into the
> labels argument of cut().
>
> Dennis
>
> On Tue, Nov 27, 2012 at 10:55 PM, dhaval <nucle...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I am trying to create a piecewise geom_smooth, that is, I am trying to
> > create difference geom_smooth curve for different portions for my x-axis.
> >
> > Using the following code:
> >
> > y = floor(runif(100,1,10))
> > df = as.data.frame(cbind(x,y))
> > rm(p)
> > p <- ggplot(df,aes(x,y))
> > p <- p + geom_line(aes(group = 1))
> > p <- p + geom_smooth(aes(df$x,df$y,group = 1, data = subset(df, x>90),
> > fullrange = FALSE))
> > p
> >
> >
> > I want to create a geom_smooth curve only for the portion that is for x > 90
> > (ideally, i would like one for each of x<30, one for 31<x<50, etc).
> >
> > I have tried various combinations, but I don't seem to know what is wrong as
> > it does not work. I still want to have a geom_line for the whole x-series,

> >
> > I get errors such as "Error: Aesthetics must either be length one, or the

> >
> > Help would be greatly appreciated,
> >
> > Thank you,
> >
> > Dhaval

messages.body_plain:
Hi Antonio,

That error message typically comes when there is some sort of mismatch in your data.  For example you could be using variables from different datasets that have an unequal number of rows.  When you see the particular values 79, 0, the zero is a give away that for some variable, there is no data.  That can cue you in to look for missing variables or misspelled variable names.  In your case, you use mean, but the variable is called mean.median.  ggplot does not find a variable mean, so there is 0 rows of data for that.  This code works for me:

ggplot(resDF, aes(x = coef.name <http://coef.name>, y = mean.median, color = model)) +

  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = low, ymax = upper),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
 labs(y = "Effect", x = "") +
 coord_flip() +
 ggtitle("Fixed effects estimates from the main model") +
 scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "orange", "forestgreen"))

Cheers,

Josh

messages.subject: Binned fill aesthetic in geom_area
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'd like to produce a frequency power spectrum with EEG data. This works fine but coloring the area below the line by frequency bands does not work so well. Here is what I'd like to achieve:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-PSwv0TlS6R4/ULc5159UlyI/AAAAAAAAALA/qOSMwrDIkT0/s1600/goal.png>

Here's a data snipped with the data which underlies the above plot:

> load(url("http://dl.dropbox.com/u/6281903/snippet.Rda"))

This is what the data looks like:

> > head(dd)
>          Hz power  band
> 1 0.9765625 0.123 delta
> 2 1.9531250 9.511 delta
> 3 2.9296875 0.777 delta
> 4 3.9062500 3.702 theta
> 5 4.8828125 5.138 theta
> 6 5.8593750 2.636 theta

The following code reduces the plot nicely but without coloring:

> ggplot(data=dd, aes(x=Hz, y=power)) +
>   geom_area() +
>   theme_bw() + xlim(0, 32) + ylab(expression(paste(µV^2/Hz)))

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-1hC2VTxaNVM/ULc6CpBdZ8I/AAAAAAAAALI/CiKy-2rLEuc/s1600/bw.png>

Adding a fill aesthetic produces gaps between the frequency bands where the data was interpolated before:

> ggplot(data=dd, aes(x=Hz, y=power)) +
>   geom_area(aes(fill=band)) +
>   scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1", na.value = NA, guide = "none") +
>   theme_bw() + xlim(0, 32) + ylab(expression(paste(µV^2/Hz)))

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-ZluXSmsdWsA/ULc6IYhBsTI/AAAAAAAAALQ/Y4tLyWg3_TI/s1600/cl.png>

Is there some way how I can fix this plot? I'm grateful for any suggestions you might have.

messages.body_plain:
I found two workarounds but only one is really an option. I could close the gaps by interpolating the area between the Hz values but the plot only looks continuous when the interpolation is really dense and that results in unreasonably huge data sets. The other option is to draw rectangles and cover the area above the line with whitespace. That is what I'm doing now, the code looks like this:

> ggplot(data=dd, aes(x=Hz, y=power)) +
>   geom_rect(xmin=subdelta[1], xmax=subdelta[2], ymin = 0, ymax = max(dd$power), fill = "grey70") +
>   geom_rect(xmin=delta[1], xmax=delta[2], ymin = 0, ymax = max(dd$power), fill = "orange") +
>   geom_rect(xmin=theta[1], xmax=theta[2], ymin = 0, ymax = max(dd$power), fill = "yellow") +
>   geom_rect(xmin=alpha[1], xmax=alpha[2], ymin = 0, ymax = max(dd$power), fill = "forestgreen") +
>   geom_rect(xmin=beta[1], xmax=beta[2] - 1, ymin = 0, ymax = max(dd$power), fill = "blue") +
>   geom_vline(x=0) + geom_hline(y=0, width = 28) +
>   geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=power), ymax=max(dd$power), fill = "white") +
>   xlim(0, beta[2]) + ylim(0, max(dd$power)) +
>   scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0,0.5)) +
>   scale_y_continuous(expand=c(0,0.05))+
>   theme_bw() +
>   theme(panel.grid.major=element_blank(),
>         panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),
